cards.title: Run a Five Dysfunctions Team Diagnostic
cards.summary: Score your leadership team against the five dysfunctions with a 15-statement questionnaire to find which layer is broken before you fix anything else.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why your ecommerce leadership team (merchandising, growth, ops, supply chain) makes slow or reversed decisions before choosing an intervention like restructuring or new hires.
steps: Have every member of the leadership team rate 15 statements on a 3/2/1 scale (3 = usually, 2 = sometimes, 1 = rarely), answering honestly and without over-thinking.

Group the scores: Trust = statements 4, 6, 12; Fear of Conflict = 1, 7, 10; Lack of Commitment = 3, 8, 13; Avoidance of Accountability = 2, 11, 14; Inattention to Results = 5, 9, 15. Total each group.

Interpret per the source's heuristics: 8–9 suggests the dysfunction is not a problem, 6–7 suggests it could be a problem, 3–5 suggests it needs to be addressed. Treat these as rough indicators, not precise measurements.
Compare members' scores rather than only averaging them — large discrepancies are themselves diagnostic of a trust problem.
Discuss the results as a team and agree on one behavioral change to test over the next quarter.
Re-run the diagnostic periodically, because the source stresses that even strong teams drift back toward dysfunction without constant work.
caveats: The scoring bands are the author's practical heuristics, not validated psychometrics; do not treat a 6 as a verdict.
Self-report scores can be gamed or unconsciously flattering; the conversation about discrepancies matters more than the number.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Model the Five Dysfunctions as a Chain, Not Five Projects
cards.summary: Trust, conflict, commitment, accountability and results are a sequential stack — breaking one link undermines the whole team, so diagnose in order rather than fixing symptoms independently.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest management effort when your ecommerce team shows several problems at once (missed launch dates, silent meetings, finger-pointing between merchandising and fulfillment).
steps: Map the chain: absence of trust → fear of conflict → lack of commitment → avoidance of accountability → inattention to results.

Check the bottom link first. If leaders hide mistakes and weaknesses, unfiltered debate about assortment, pricing or promo plans will not happen, and any 'commitment' is feigned agreement in the meeting.
Trace a current failure backward through the chain — e.g. a launch that slipped because nobody challenged an unrealistic date, because nobody trusted the person who owned it.
Address the lowest broken link first instead of launching an accountability program on top of a trust problem.
State the positive behaviors you want instead: trust one another, debate ideas unfiltered, commit to decisions, hold peers accountable, focus on collective results.
caveats: The model is the source's framework, not an empirically proven causal chain; treat ordering as a practical heuristic.
The source notes the behaviors are simple in theory but demand discipline and persistence that few teams sustain, so expect months, not weeks.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Behavioral Signs That Distinguish Trusting From Distrusting Teams
cards.summary: Compare your team's observable behaviors against the source's lists of trust symptoms to decide whether the problem is a trust deficit or something else.
cards.use_when: Assessing your ecommerce leadership or cross-functional team (e.g. growth, merchandising and supply chain) after a pattern of stalled decisions or unusual turnover.
steps: Look for the distrust markers the source lists: concealing weaknesses and mistakes, hesitating to ask for or offer help, jumping to conclusions about others' intentions, failing to tap colleagues' expertise, spending time managing how one appears, holding grudges, dreading meetings.

Look for the trust markers: admitting mistakes, asking for help, accepting questions about one's own area, giving the benefit of the doubt before reaching a negative conclusion, offering feedback and assistance, offering and accepting apologies without hesitation, looking forward to working together.
Score which side the majority of observed behavior falls on for your team, and note specific incidents rather than impressions.
If distrust dominates, avoid jumping straight to accountability or results initiatives; build trust first.
caveats: The source's lists are practitioner observations, not a validated instrument.
Distrust is expensive in ways that are hard to measure directly (the source argues it consumes time and energy better spent on the work), so resist demands for a hard ROI before acting.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Define Trust as Vulnerability, Not Reliability
cards.summary: Team trust means peers are confident each other's intentions are good enough to be open about weaknesses and mistakes — predictability alone is not enough.
cards.use_when: Evaluating why your ecommerce team avoids surfacing bad news about a failing SKU, a vendor delay, or a campaign that underperformed, even when individuals reliably deliver their assigned work.
steps: Separate the two meanings of trust: (a) predictability based on past delivery, and (b) vulnerability-based trust — the confidence that you can expose weaknesses, skill gaps, mistakes and requests for help without it being used against you.
Recognize that high performers often learned to be competitive and protective of their reputations, so turning that instinct off for the team is a real cost they must choose to pay.
Ask directly in a team setting whether people can admit an error without damage; the answer is the diagnostic.
Model it: leaders and senior operators should be the first to name their own mistake or gap.
Note that distrust shows up as time spent being strategically political and managing how one appears, not just as interpersonal friction.
caveats: The source stresses this is difficult and slow — vulnerability-based trust requires shared experience over time, repeated follow-through and understanding of individuals' unique attributes.
Distinguish carefully: reliability is still needed; the point is that it is insufficient for a cohesive team.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Personal Histories Exercise for Faster Team Trust
cards.summary: A sub-hour, low-risk exercise where team members share non-sensitive biographical facts to build empathy and prevent unfair behavioral attributions.
cards.use_when: Kicking off a newly formed ecommerce leadership team, integrating a new head of merchandising or supply chain, or restarting a burned-out cross-functional group after a bad quarter.
steps: In a meeting, go around the table and have each person answer a short list of low-sensitivity questions: number of siblings, hometown, unique childhood challenges, favorite hobbies, first job, worst job.
Keep it moderately personal but not overly sensitive; the goal is relatability, not disclosure of private struggles.
Run it as a discussion, not a form; the value comes from hearing each other, not from the answers themselves.
Expect this to take at least 30 minutes.
Follow up by scheduling regular working sessions where the resulting familiarity can be reinforced, because the source warns trust erodes without continued interaction.
Apply it specifically to dependencies your team has — e.g. the person who forecasts demand learning how the marketing lead came to their role can soften routine interdepartmental friction.
caveats: This is a first step, not a trust program; the source says vulnerability-based trust cannot be achieved overnight and requires shared experiences over time.
The author states these exercises must be paired with regular follow-up in daily work, or momentum is lost.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Team Effectiveness Exercise: One Contribution, One Needed Improvement
cards.summary: Each member names the single most important contribution a peer makes and the one thing that peer must improve or stop, reported one person at a time starting with the leader.
cards.use_when: When a team is functional enough to handle direct feedback but still has unspoken performance or behavior problems — for example, a merchandising lead whose dismissiveness is quietly degrading planning meetings.
steps: Frame it: every member will identify, for each peer, the single most important contribution they make to the team and the one area they must improve or eliminate for the team's good.
Start with the team leader so the leader is subject to the same scrutiny first, setting the norm.
Take one person at a time, with all responses reported while that person listens and does not defend.
Keep each pass tight — the source reports that roughly an hour is enough for a team, yielding both constructive and positive information.
Follow up on each identified development area in subsequent one-on-ones so it does not become a one-off exercise.
Book at least 60 minutes minimum.
caveats: The source acknowledges this is more rigorous and riskier than the personal histories exercise; it may feel intrusive and dangerous at first.
It assumes some baseline trust; the source notes even relatively dysfunctional teams can often make it work with surprisingly little tension, but results vary.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Use Personality Profiles to Reduce Team Friction
cards.summary: Behavioral preference profiles such as the MBTI give nonjudgmental descriptions of how people think, speak and act, making peer friction easier to interpret and manage.
cards.use_when: When recurring clashes between, say, a data-driven growth lead and an intuitive brand/creative lead are being read as personal conflict instead of stylistic difference.
steps: Choose a profiling tool that is nonjudgmental (no type is better than another), research-based rather than astrology-like, and in which participants actively identify their own type rather than receiving a verdict from a printout or score.
The author's stated preference is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator; a number of alternatives are also used by different audiences.
Have the whole team complete it and share results openly, then discuss how each type tends to communicate, decide and handle disagreement.
Use the shared vocabulary in live disagreements to reframe stylistic clashes before they become personal.
Revisit profiles when new members join, as the source shows for a new marketing VP who was walked through the model and then had his Myers-Briggs results reviewed with him.
Budget at least four hours of minimum time for these tools.
caveats: The source notes many such tools require a licensed consultant, which it says matters to avoid misuse of their implications.
Profiles explain style, not competence; the author positions them as trust-building and conflict-handling aids, not performance verdicts.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Keep 360-Degree Feedback Out of Compensation
cards.summary: A 360-degree program works only if it is a pure development tool, divorced entirely from pay and formal performance evaluation.
cards.use_when: Rolling out peer feedback across ecommerce functions (merchandising, marketing, ops) and deciding whether it will feed into reviews or salary decisions.
steps: Separate the program from any compensation or formal evaluation link; the source says even a slight connection invites dangerous political undertones.
Position it explicitly as developmental: it lets people identify strengths and weaknesses with no repercussions.
Brief participants before collecting input so they understand the firewall from pay and ratings.
Use outputs to design individual development plans and follow-up conversations, not scores in a review file.
Repeat annually or on a cycle rather than continuously, so it remains a deliberate exercise rather than a constant channel for criticism.
caveats: The author flags this as riskier than other trust tools because peers make specific judgments and deliver constructive criticism directly.
Without the firewall from compensation, the source expects the program to become political and lose its developmental value.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Vulnerability Must Start With the Leader — And Cannot Be Staged
cards.summary: The leader must go first in exposing weakness, create an environment that does not punish it, and never fake it for effect.
cards.use_when: When you, as founder or ecommerce lead, want the team to surface bad news about a channel, a vendor, or an assortment bet earlier — but the team still filters what they tell you.
steps: Open with a genuine disclosure of a mistake or limitation of your own, before asking anyone else to be open.

Watch for subtle punishment of vulnerability — interrupting, sarcasm, or sidelining someone after they admit a failure — and stop it immediately, because the source argues even well-intentioned teams discourage trust this way.
Do not perform vulnerability as a technique; the source states one of the best ways to lose a team's trust is to feign vulnerability to manipulate others' emotions.
Choose disclosures that are real and relevant to work rather than manufactured personal drama.
Reinforce vulnerability by continuing to ask for input on your own decisions and by visibly acting on what you learn.
caveats: The source is a business fable-style treatment; the leader-first rule is a stated principle, not an experimentally verified threshold.
Exposure carries real risk in the short term — the author frames it as risking face so subordinates will take the same risk.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Distinguish Productive Ideological Conflict From Personal Attack
cards.summary: Healthy conflict is confined to concepts and ideas and may look passionate or emotional from outside, while personality-focused attacks are destructive and should be ruled out.
cards.use_when: Setting norms for how your ecommerce team debates pricing changes, discount depth, channel budget or a new bundle — before the next planning meeting.
steps: Agree the rule: debate is about concepts and ideas; personality-focused and mean-spirited attacks are out.

Expect passion, emotion and frustration in legitimate debate, and do not intervene merely because it looks heated; the source says an outside observer could mistake productive conflict for unproductive discord.
Judge by outcome: good conflict ends quickly with the best available answer and no residual resentment, and leaves people ready for the next issue.
Treat avoidance as the real risk — the source argues suppressed disagreement pushes people into back-channel personal attacks, which are nastier than open argument over issues.
Stop the common practice of taking contested topics 'off-line' as a euphemism for deferring them indefinitely.
caveats: The line between passionate debate and personal attack is often only clear in retrospect; the purpose test (best solution in the shortest time) is the source's proposed standard.
The source notes conflict is taboo at work and gets harder to permit the higher up the management chain you go, so norms must be actively maintained.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Assign a Miner of Conflict to Surface Buried Disagreements
cards.summary: Designate someone in each meeting to extract buried disagreements and force the team to work through them, staying in the discussion until resolution.
cards.use_when: Running an ecommerce planning or S&OP-style meeting where unresolved issues (inventory commitments, promo calendar, channel budget) keep resurfacing instead of being settled.
steps: Recognize the symptom: issues that reappear meeting after meeting without resolution usually mean the real disagreement was never surfaced.
Assign the miner role for a given meeting or discussion — a person whose job is to call out sensitive issues and push the team to work through them.
Require the miner to stay objective and to commit to staying with the conflict until it resolves, rather than letting the group move on.
Rotate or specify who holds the role so it does not become one person's permanent burden.
Close the loop by recording the resolution and the specific calls to action.
caveats: This takes courage and confidence from the person holding the role; in low-trust teams it can be read as aggression.
The source presents it as a technique for teams that tend to avoid conflict, not a universal meeting requirement.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Use 'Real-Time Permission' to Keep Difficult Debates Going
cards.summary: When people start retreating from heated debate, interrupt to tell them the discomfort is appropriate and to keep going — then confirm afterward that the conflict was healthy.
cards.use_when: Facilitating a contentious ecommerce decision — cutting a channel, changing a returns policy, repricing a hero SKU — and watching participants soften their position to reduce tension.
steps: Watch for body language and speech that signal discomfort: hedging, apologizing for a point, or dropping a position mid-argument.
Interrupt briefly to explicitly grant permission: state that this level of disagreement is necessary and expected, and that they should continue.
Let the debate continue rather than resolving it yourself; the source notes this drains tension and gives participants confidence to keep going.
After the meeting, remind the group that the conflict they just had was good for the team and not something to avoid.
Note the source's observation that nobody fully gets used to conflict; if it is not a little uncomfortable, it is probably not real.
Keep the leader's protective instinct in check — the source warns leaders often interrupt disagreements prematurely and rob people of the chance to build conflict-management skills.
caveats: The source acknowledges it can sound paternal; it describes it as remarkably effective but not a fixed protocol.
Overprotective intervention is the specific failure mode the author warns against for leaders promoting healthy conflict.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Use the Thomas-Kilmann Instrument for Conflict Style Awareness
cards.summary: The TKI helps team members see their default approach to conflict so they can choose tactics deliberately rather than reflexively.
cards.use_when: When the same ecommerce peers repeatedly collide in the same way (e.g. one always yields on assortment calls, another always competes and forces a winner) and you want to change the pattern.
steps: Have team members complete the Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument.
Review each person's dominant modes and discuss when each mode is appropriate — competing, avoiding, compromising, accommodating, collaborating.
In live debate, name the mode being used and ask whether it is the right choice for this issue.
Use the shared vocabulary instead of attributing recurring friction to personality.
Pair this with other behavioral-preference tools, since the source notes most personality instruments describe how different types handle conflict.
caveats: This addresses conflict style only; on its own it will not fix a trust deficit underneath.
The source treats it as a supporting tool, mentioning it in one paragraph rather than prescribing a full procedure.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Separate Conflict About Issues From Your Team's Job
cards.summary: Leaders arguing about issues in a meeting is the work, not a symptom — resolving it there prevents pushing unsolvable problems down to their teams.
cards.use_when: A leadership meeting over the sales budget, headcount or channel investment turns tense and someone argues the team has regressed.
steps: Reframe the moment: when leaders debate an issue rather than attack each other, that is the healthy conflict you have been trying to build.
Recognize that letting leaders hash out these disagreements gives their teams clear direction instead of forcing subordinates to solve problems they have no authority to solve.
Confirm the disagreement is about the issue — e.g. whether to add sales headcount versus controlling quota inflation — rather than about which person is right.
Land the decision and communicate it down as clear direction, so the debate translates into action rather than lingering ambiguity.
Expect residual discomfort; the source shows participants reporting it still feels like fighting even when it is productive.
caveats: The source's example includes a direct clash between two executives that initially alarmed the rest of the team, illustrating that intensity alone is not a failure signal.
Do not use this framing to excuse personal attacks; the distinction between issue conflict and interpersonal conflict still applies.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Prepare the Team for the Dip After Early Progress
cards.summary: Warn the team explicitly that progress will be invisible in results for a while, and that groups often slide backward, so early behavioral wins are not mistaken for a finished job.
cards.use_when: Right after an offsite or process reset, before the next quarter's numbers land — so the ecommerce team does not revert when channel performance and morale still look flat.
steps: Tell the team directly that there will be days they will wonder if anything changed, and that behavioral change takes longer than a few weeks to show up in the bottom line.
State plainly that teams further along have slid backward, so discipline and persistence are the actual risk factors.

Keep the pace up after the initial burst: the source shows the leader continued to push on behavior — calling out smugness in meetings, forcing a peer to confront the team about unresponsiveness, and working through budget fights late into the night.
Track leading behavioral signals rather than only financial results in the interim — for example, whether people stay together during breaks and whether meetings are louder and more animated.
Treat laughter and eagerness to schedule follow-up as informal progress markers, as the source does for a recovering team.
caveats: The source is a fable; the observation that the team laughed more and stayed together is anecdotal, not a measured benchmark.
Optimism should be tempered deliberately — the author has the leader 'let the air out of the balloon' precisely to avoid over-confidence.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Address Individual Behavior Problems Directly, With Specific Evidence
cards.summary: When a leader's behavior is damaging the team, name it plainly and concretely, tolerate the emotional response, and hold the behavioral requirement firm.
cards.use_when: Handling a genuinely damaging team member — a merchandising or marketing lead whose dismissiveness is undermining peers — and deciding whether to attempt a turnaround or an exit.
steps: Go directly to the core issue at the start: state that the person is not a fit for the team and does not appear to want to be there, rather than opening with tangential feedback.

When they ask for the basis, give specific, observed behavior rather than general impressions — the source's example lists eye-rolling, disrespectful remarks toward a peer, and refusal to attend a company priority training.
Expect shock and denial. The source shows the person may genuinely not see it, or may be being coy; either way, repeat the specifics calmly.
Handle the counter-moves: blame-shifting (peers don't respect me), escalation threats (referencing the board or legal action), and claims that the behavior would change elsewhere.
Make the actual requirement clear — either complete and fast behavioral change or departure — and acknowledge honestly that you are not sure they want to do it.
Do not volunteer concessions in the room; the source shows the leader deliberately said she would see what she could do rather than immediately agreeing to a severance and equity request.
If it ends in departure, get a real agreement: severance, vesting and the official record, worked out with HR.
caveats: This is a fable; the dialogue is illustrative and the specific severance and equity terms are not a template.
The source frames the leader's job as building a functioning team, not avoiding board confrontation, which is a strong stance stated by the character.
Candid feedback of the harshest kind (such as telling the person they seem bitter) is the character's choice, not a recommended universal script.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Defend High Performers' Behavior, Not Just Their Output
cards.summary: Tolerating a high producer's destructive behavior makes the manager — not the individual — responsible for the team's performance collapse.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to protect a top-performing ecommerce buyer, media buyer or engineer whose poor collaboration is driving colleagues out.
steps: Watch the pattern the source describes: a top performer produces better work than anyone, peers complain repeatedly, the manager half-heartedly addresses it and then shields the performer because output looks good.
Recognize the second-order effects: other people's load increases, morale deteriorates, and the department's overall output declines even though the star is still producing.
Refuse to resolve the tension by rewarding the behavior — in the source's cautionary story, the manager promoted the difficult performer, and three of seven analysts quit within two weeks.
Attribute the performance problem to your tolerance of the behavior, not to the individual alone.
Decide early: either the behavior changes, or the person goes — the source's story has performance improving dramatically within a month of the person's departure, even with three fewer staff.
caveats: The story is a fable with a dramatic outcome; do not read the reported 50 percent productivity impact or the one-month recovery as measured benchmarks.
The source's lesson is specifically that manager tolerance is the causal factor, which may overstate the individual leader's role in complex team outcomes.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Let Departures Be Mourned, Then Reframe the Decision
cards.summary: Even the removal of a difficult team member triggers mourning and self-doubt among peers; address it openly rather than letting it dampen the work.
cards.use_when: After terminating or losing a senior ecommerce leader, and noticing the leadership team's energy and meeting quality drop in the following days.
steps: Name the elephant explicitly in the next team meeting and ask how people feel about the departure.
Expect the standard concerns: fear of losing another executive, worry about the function, and the question of who is next.

Resist defending the departed person's performance record in order to avoid a fight — the source's leader wanted to argue that the person was never really part of the team but stayed quiet and listened first.

Answer with a personal story of a comparable mistake if you have one; the source's leader told a story about tolerating a destructive top performer and being fired herself, concluding 'they fired the right person.'
Land the message that the departure was done to protect the team: 'I don't plan on losing any of you.'
Expect a symbolic reaction beyond the individual — the source notes employee concern after a departure often reflects what the change signals rather than the loss of that specific person.
caveats: The story's device is a leader sharing a career failure; the specific narrative is illustrative, not a required script.
Mourning a difficult colleague's departure is described as nearly universal by the source, even when the person was the source of the problem.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Sequence the Communication After a Senior Departure
cards.summary: Announce a departure plainly to the team, hold legal detail back, and handle employee and press messaging with a single consistent line.
cards.use_when: Managing the internal and external messaging after a senior ecommerce leader leaves — before employees hear it from someone else or a trade publication calls.
steps: Tell the leadership team first, and state the confidentiality basis in advance because of legal issues related to departed employees.
Give a direct reason without unnecessary detail: the person was unwilling to adjust behavior and it was hurting the team, so you asked them to leave.
Answer the practical questions the team will actually ask: how the person took it, what happens to the function, what employees and press will be told.
For the function, name the interim plan — look for a successor while extending responsibility to strong internal people — and express confidence in that plan.
For employees and press, use one simple line: the person is moving on. The source stresses there is little flexibility about disclosing sensitive information.
Do not let initial reactions drive the message; the source argues that if the team makes visible progress, employees and analysts will settle, and many employees will not be surprised at all.
caveats: The source's example is a story; legal and disclosure obligations vary by jurisdiction and should involve counsel and HR.
The claim that employees 'won't be that surprised' is a character's expectation, not a measured outcome.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Run an Internal vs External Succession Debate, Then Decide
cards.summary: Have the team debate the replacement decision openly, then make the call yourself and state the criteria the hire must demonstrate.
cards.use_when: Filling a senior ecommerce vacancy — head of marketing, merchandising or supply chain — when there is pressure to promote internally from the existing team.
steps: Let the team debate whether to promote one of the departed leader's direct reports or hire externally, and let the disagreement run rather than shutting it down.
Before deciding, explicitly invite final input: ask whether anyone has anything else to add.

Make the call and explain the criterion you used — the source's leader said she wanted someone who could grow the department and help with branding, and saw no internal candidate close to that right now.
State the hiring bar in team terms: candidates must demonstrate trust, engage in conflict, commit to group decisions, hold peers accountable, and focus on team results rather than personal ego.
Involve the team in the search rather than keeping it with the leader — the source has every member interview candidates.
Assign a single owner to organize the search.
caveats: The source's leader overrode a divided team; this is one situational choice, and the text does not establish that external hiring is generally better.
A public statement that no internal candidate is ready can damage morale; the source does not address that risk.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Onboard a New Executive Through the Team, Not a Manual
cards.summary: Have existing team members each teach one dysfunction to the newcomer, then review working style and launch into real debates immediately.
cards.use_when: Integrating a new senior hire — a marketing, supply chain or growth leader — into an established leadership team.
steps: Assign different existing members to explain one dysfunction each, so the whole team participates in the onboarding rather than the leader delivering a presentation.
Cover the team's operating mechanics: each peer's role and responsibilities and the collective goals.
Review the newcomer's personality or behavioral-preference profile alongside the team's, and explain how peers tend to work and disagree.
Move straight into live work: the source has the team launch into passionate debates on the same day, ending them with crystal-clear agreements and no lingering bitterness.
Let the newcomer observe peers holding each other accountable directly, and keep bringing discussions back to results if tension rises.
caveats: The source is a fable; the very quick integration described is illustrative and depends on the team already functioning well.
A new hire may find direct peer confrontation uncomfortable at first; the source shows that discomfort coexisting with enthusiasm to join.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Shrink the Top Team as the Company Grows
cards.summary: A larger company generally needs a smaller executive team — add layers and move functional leaders under a COO instead of expanding the CEO's direct reports.
cards.use_when: Your ecommerce company has grown past roughly a couple of hundred employees and the leadership meeting has become too large for fluid, substantive discussion.
steps: Count your direct reports and test whether the group is still small enough for real debate; the source's leader found nine around a table unworkable even with a cooperative team.
Consolidate: the source example moved two functional leaders under a COO, moved HR under the CFO, and ended with five direct reports — CTO, CFO, COO, VP marketing, VP business development.
Explain changes individually and confidently to each affected person rather than announcing them cold in a group.
Expect status concerns even from reasonable people; in the source, the team's first reaction to a founder no longer reporting to the CEO was worry about his disappointment.
Note that the reorganization can be initiated by the affected person if the logic is sound — in the source, the board member himself proposed reporting to the COO.
caveats: The 'larger company, smaller top team' rule is the source's stated belief, not a measured threshold; the specific headcount and reporting structure come from the story's example.
Reducing direct reports can feel like a demotion; the source shows that peers will raise this concern, so address it explicitly.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx
